what_its_for: Rucaparib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer, or primary peritoneal cancer. It is also used to treat a type of prostate cancer. Your doctor prescribes it when your cancer has certain gene changes (called BRCA mutations) or when other treatments have not worked well enough.
how_to_take: Take rucaparib by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or split them. Try to take your doses at the same times every day to help you remember. If you vomit after taking a dose, do not take an extra dose — just take your next scheduled dose as planned.
dosing: Your doctor will tell you exactly how many tablets to take and how often. The usual dose is twice a day (once in the morning and once in the evening), about 12 hours apart. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be adjusted based on how your body responds or if you have side effects.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose at your regularly scheduled time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store rucaparib tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep them in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Store away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming pregnant while taking rucaparib, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. If you are male and have a partner who could become pregnant, use condoms during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for 2 weeks after stopping. Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges, as they may affect how the medicine works in your body. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some can interact with rucaparib.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice any of the following: unusual tiredness or weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, or fast heartbeat (signs of low blood cell counts); unusual bruising or bleeding; fever, chills, or signs of infection; new or worsening bone pain; confusion, memory problems, or seizures; blood in your urine or pain when urinating; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; or any new or unusual symptoms that worry you. Also tell your doctor if you are scheduled for any blood tests, as regular monitoring is needed during treatment.
when_it_works: Rucaparib does not cure cancer, but it works to slow or stop cancer growth. Some people notice improvement within the first few months, but your doctor will monitor your progress with regular tests and check-ups. It is important to keep taking the medicine as prescribed even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use rucaparib if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can be harmful. Kidney or liver problems: Your dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney or liver disease — make sure your doctor knows about any such conditions. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, so your doctor will monitor you carefully. Children: Rucaparib is not approved for use in children.
